abstract: Can an integrated optical readout improve the useful operating range of a miniature microphone? We address this question with an analytical model of a diaphragm carrying the sensing arm of a Mach-Zehnder interferometer (MZI). The model links pressure-induced bending to waveguide elongation and then to photocurrent, allowing mechanical sensitivity and optical detection limits to be assessed separately. Optical shot noise and back-cavity thermomechanical noise set the pressure resolution, while a 10% total harmonic distortion criterion defines acoustic overload. Two operating regimes are examined: a compact MEMS microphone with 1 mW optical input and a measurement microphone with 100 mW optical input. For the compact case, a 1 mm diameter, 1 micrometer thick, stress-free silicon diaphragm and 100% modulation efficiency give a predicted signal-to-noise ratio of 78 dB and acoustic overload pressure of 124 dB. The higher-power case lowers the modeled noise floor and increases dynamic range relative to the selected measurement microphone benchmark. These estimates rely on favorable assumptions and do not establish a substantial overall advantage in conventional microphone applications. Remote optical interrogation offers a separate motivation for harsh-environment sensing, but the temperature tolerance of the proposed sensing head remains unverified. The analysis identifies the design tradeoffs and measurements needed to test the predicted performance.
